title: Republicans mulling deal that would fund military, but limit operations in Iran | CNN Politics
text:
Source: CNN

In the final days of the GOP’s complete power in Washington, there’s a real chance the Pentagon might not get another dollar this year – unless Republican lawmakers strike a deal with Democrats to rein in Trump’s ability to attack Iran.

Top Senate Democrats and Republicans are engaged inhigh-stakes talksabout cutting off funding for future offensive operations in the Iran war in exchange for replenishing the tens of billions that the Department of Defense has said is urgently needed, according to multiple lawmakers and aides in both parties.

The push faces enormous obstacles in a bitterly divided Congress, with Republicans largely wary of crossing President Donald Trump on the war – even after their midterm losses – and emboldened Democrats seeking big restrictions on his power.

But if no deal is reached, the Pentagon has almost no other chance of getting the money this year. And that means they’d have to ask Democrats for the money next year — an even tougher task, when every House Democrat voted to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth earlier this month.

“I think there’s a way for Democrats to make their point without tying the hands of the commander in chief and the defense of our country,” Senate Armed Services Chairman Roger Wicker told CNN on Friday when asked about the emerging proposal.

Talks are in the early stages, and there are still major questions about exactly what any restrictions would look like, and what else could be included, such as funding for Ukraine’s war against Russia. Sources in both parties have said it’s not yet clear if there’s a way for Republicans to accept Democrats’ demands without hampering the US military’s ability to keep troops safe – and without infuriating Trump.

“I think there is a room for negotiation there, and it would have to be something that the administration would find acceptable, too,” said GOP Sen. John Hoeven of North Dakota, who is in talks with both Democrats and the White House on the matter. “But again, we want to deal, we want to end the conflict from a position of strength, and we need to fund the military.”

Some Senate Democrats hope they can convince Trump and GOP leaders to put a proposal into next month’s stopgap funding bill. If that did not pass, it would mean a debilitating shutdown at a time when Republicans still control all of Washington.

But several Republicans said they fear the talks could shift yet again if and when Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer wins a contested leadership election on December 1. They believe the looming contest has led him to strike such a firm posture on defunding the Iran war. (Several noted that House Democrats have privately struck a different tone, very eager to avoid a shutdown and suggesting they’re willing to punt the Iran issue to 2027, according to multiple sources in both parties.)

Still, many Republicans believe they have no real options, other than striking a deal with Democrats on next month’s funding bill, since they don’t have the votes to do it on a party-line basis.

At least one Republican, Sen. Josh Hawley of Missouri, told CNN on Friday he is open to supporting a compromise.

More military funding has been a key priority for the White House. Top Pentagon officials have spent months lobbying Congress for more money in the middle of a war with Iran — including personal calls from Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, countless closed-door briefings and treks to Camp David.

Privately, though, GOP lawmakers and aides say that Pentagon officials have hurt their own chances by repeatedly misleading lawmakers about the true need for the funds. Defense officials have sent over four separate funding requests — including one just this week — that have made it difficult to discern the most urgent priorities, according to multiple people familiar with the discussions.

“I can add up four numbers, so don’t think you’re tricking me by dividing it into different buckets, and so that is a frustration,” lamented Democratic Sen. Tim Kaine of Virginia, who is on the Armed Services Committee, about the various funding requests.

CNN has reached out to the Defense Department for comment.

The administration has been making a stronger case in recent days, according to sources. Senate Republicans heard a strong pitch from Deputy Defense Secretary Steve Feinberg at a closed-door meeting this week, and House Republicans are expected to hear from him in the coming days.

Kaine, who’s been a vocal advocate of ending the war while supporting US troops, has made clear that Democrats are not opposed to all of the Pentagon’s funding requests. But he also doesn’t consider most of them to be urgent.

“Most of what they’re seeking is important and needed, but not needed tomorrow. Because like munitions replacement, you put money in, you’re not going to get to munitions for some time. So this isn’t necessarily about tomorrow,” Kaine said. “Some of those priorities in the $350 [billion request] are needed, and you would find an openness to some of our other side.”

CNN’s Morgan Rimmer, Ted Barrett and Arlette Saenz contributed to this report.

CNN’s Morgan Rimmer, Ted Barrett and Arlette Saenz contributed to this report.
